questions.q: How did new dynasties emerge from among the samantas in early medieval India?
answer: By the seventh century, powerful landlords and warrior chiefs were recognised by existing kings as subordinate rulers called samantas.

answer.text: A samanta who gained wealth and military strength was given higher titles such as maha-samanta or maha-mandaleshvara, and offered gifts and service to his overlord.

When strong enough, some samantas broke free of their overlords and set up their own kingdoms. The Rashtrakutas of the Deccan, once subordinate to the Chalukyas, are a clear example: in the mid-eighth century Dantidurga overthrew his overlord.
To legitimise such rule, he performed the hiranya-garbha ritual, believed to turn the sacrificer into a kshatriya. Thus new dynasties rose from within the old political order.

questions.q: Describe the main achievements of the Chola rulers.
answer: The Cholas, rising from the fertile Kaveri delta, built one of the most powerful kingdoms of the south.

answer.text: Vijayalaya captured Thanjavur in the mid-ninth century; Rajaraja I greatly expanded the empire; and Rajendra I led expeditions up to the Ganga and across the sea against Srivijaya in Southeast Asia, founding Gangaikonda-cholapuram.
Rajaraja I built the magnificent Rajarajeshvara (Brihadeshwara) temple at Thanjavur, and the Cholas produced superb bronze images, above all the dancing Nataraja.
Their villages had famous self-governing assemblies — the sabha, ur and nagaram — whose working is recorded in the Uttaramerur inscriptions.

questions.q: Describe the system of local self-government in Chola villages.
answer: Chola villages enjoyed a remarkable degree of local self-government through assemblies of landholders and merchants.

answer.text: The ur was the assembly of non-Brahmana landowners; the sabha was the assembly of Brahmana landholders in villages granted to Brahmanas (brahmadeya); and the nagaram was the association of merchants.
The sabha worked through committees that looked after irrigation, gardens, temples and justice.
The Uttaramerur inscriptions describe how members were chosen: names of eligible people were written on palm-leaf tickets, put into a pot, and drawn by lot — the kudavolai system.

answer: This made the Chola countryside one of the best-documented examples of early local democracy.
